lessons.title: Mean, median, mode and choosing a centre
lessons.summary: Calculate the complete measures of centre and choose a summary that answers the actual statistical question.
lessons.objective: Calculate the complete measures of centre and choose a summary that answers the actual statistical question.
lessons.before: Order data, read a frequency table and retain exact fractions. Mixed-topic written tasks also use descriptive variance and SD, introduced in the first lesson.
lessons.ideas:
Mean, median and mode answer different questions

\[\bar{x}=\frac{\sum x}{n}.\]

The mean uses every numerical observation. Find the median only after ordering the data: for even n average the two central observations. The mode is the most frequent observed value. Give every tied mode when the greatest frequency exceeds one; if all values occur once, this chapter uses the convention of no mode.

A modal class uses density when widths differ

For grouped continuous data the book defines the modal class as the class with greatest frequency density. The class with the greatest frequency can be different. With equal widths both comparisons agree; if all densities are equal there is no unique modal class.

Choose in context

The median is less affected by the size of an extreme observation. The mean can be useful when a total matters; the mode can describe the most common category. Do not declare one measure universally best. Explain what typical means in the question.

Descriptive spread primer for mixed tasks

\[\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2},\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}.\]

Use divisor n here, not n−1. SD has the original units; variance has squared units. Some written questions deliberately combine this chapter with Measures of variation. A correct centre does not by itself establish consistency.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the observation count, measurement units and requested measure.
  2. Keep exact totals and distinguish raw values from grouped estimates.
  3. Restore every original count, coding or value condition.
  4. State the complete result and justify a contextual choice separately.
mistakes: Do not confuse the median position with its observed value.
List every tied mode, not just the first one noticed.
Unequal-width modal classes require density.
A high outlier does not automatically invalidate the mean for every purpose.

examples.title: Three different measures from one ordered set
examples.question: Find the mean, median and mode of 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 13.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=\frac{42}{6}=7,\\\text{median}&=\frac{5+7}{2}=6,\\\text{mode}&=5.\end{aligned}\]

The median is the average of the third and fourth ordered values, not the third value alone.

examples.title: A tied mode and no mode are different cases
examples.question: State the modes of 2, 2, 4, 4, 7, 9. Then consider 2, 4, 7, 9 with no repeats.
examples.solution: The first set has two modes, 2 and 4, each occurring twice. In the second set every value occurs once, so there is no mode under the stated convention.

examples.title: An extreme value affects the mean more than the median
examples.question: Repair times are 8, 9, 10, 12 and 81 minutes. Compare mean and median as summaries of a typical repair.
examples.solution:
\[\bar{x}=\frac{120}{5}=24,\qquad\text{median}=10.\]

The mean reflects the total time, including the very long repair. For a typical individual repair, the median is less influenced by that extreme duration.

examples.title: The most frequent class is not always the modal class
examples.question:
ClassFrequency
0 ≤ x < 58
5 ≤ x < 1512
15 ≤ x < 206

Find the modal class and the greatest-frequency class.
examples.solution: Densities are \(\frac85,\frac65,\frac65\). The modal class is \([0,5)\), while the greatest frequency is in \([5,15)\). Heights identify density, areas identify frequency.

lessons.title: Coded data, scale changes and unknown observations
lessons.summary: Undo a coding in the correct direction and use separate moment equations to recover missing information.
lessons.objective: Undo a coding in the correct direction and use separate moment equations to recover missing information.
lessons.before: Order data, read a frequency table and retain exact fractions. Mixed-topic written tasks also use descriptive variance and SD, introduced in the first lesson.
lessons.ideas:
Translation changes the mean, not the spread

If \(u=x-a\), then

\[\begin{aligned}\sum x&=na+\sum u,\\\bar{x}&=a+\bar{u},\\\sigma_x&=\sigma_u.\end{aligned}\]

A coded sum is not the original sum unless the offset is zero.

Scaling affects SD by an absolute multiplier

If \(u=(x-a)/b\), write \(x=a+bu\) before decoding:

\[\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=a+b\bar{u},\\\sigma_x&=|b|\sigma_u,\\\sigma_x^2&=b^2\sigma_u^2.\end{aligned}\]

A negative multiplier reverses order but does not produce a negative SD.

Two origins can reveal a missing count

\[\sum(x-a)-\sum(x-b)=n(b-a).\]

Each observation contributes the same difference. Check that the recovered count is a positive integer before using it.

A sum and a square-sum give different information

Two unknown observations usually need two independent conditions. Recover both their sum and the sum of their squares, solve the resulting quadratic and restore the requested ordering. Do not confuse \(\sum x^2\) with \((\sum x)^2\).
lessons.method:
1. Identify the observation count, measurement units and requested measure.
  2. Keep exact totals and distinguish raw values from grouped estimates.
  3. Restore every original count, coding or value condition.
  4. State the complete result and justify a contextual choice separately.
mistakes: Undo the coding rather than applying it again.
Use the absolute scale factor for SD.
Two unknown observations need more than a sum alone.
Check integer counts, ordering and original moment conditions.

examples.title: Recover an original mean and SD from a translation
examples.question: For \(u=x-40\), \(n=8\), \(\sum u=12\), \(\sum u^2=50\). Find the original mean and SD.
examples.solution:
\[\bar{x}=40+\frac{12}{8}=41.5.\]\[\sigma_x=\sqrt{\frac{50}{8}-\left(\frac{12}{8}\right)^2}=2.\]

The translation adds 40 to the mean and leaves the SD unchanged.

examples.title: Decode the scale as well as the origin
examples.question: For \(u=(x-20)/3\), \(n=5\), \(\sum u=10\), \(\sum u^2=30\). Find the original mean and SD.
examples.solution: \[\bar{u}=2,\quad\sigma_u^2=6-4=2.\]\[\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=20+3(2)=26,\\\sigma_x&=3\sqrt2.\end{aligned}\]

examples.title: Two coded sums determine the sample size
examples.question: Given \(\sum(x-10)=30\) and \(\sum(x-15)=-10\), find n and the mean.
examples.solution:
\[30-(-10)=5n\quad\Rightarrow\quad n=8.\]\[\begin{aligned}\sum x&=30+10(8)=110,\\\bar{x}&=\frac{55}{4}.\end{aligned}\]

The difference of the two totals counts the same offset once per observation.

examples.title: Recover two missing observations
examples.question: Six observations have mean 6 and square-sum 256. Four values are 2, 4, 7, 9. Find the remaining a and b with \(a
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}a+b&=36-22=14,\\a^2+b^2&=256-150=106.\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{gathered}a^2+(14-a)^2=106\\\Rightarrow\quad a=5\text{ or }9.\end{gathered}\]

With the specified order, \((a,b)=(5,9)\). Both moment conditions are satisfied.

lessons.title: Frequency tables, grouped estimates and median interpolation
lessons.summary: Use frequencies as counts, midpoints only as a model, and cumulative positions to locate a median.
lessons.objective: Use frequencies as counts, midpoints only as a model, and cumulative positions to locate a median.
lessons.before: Order data, read a frequency table and retain exact fractions. Mixed-topic written tasks also use descriptive variance and SD, introduced in the first lesson.
lessons.ideas:
A frequency table still represents individual observations

\[n=\sum f,\qquad\bar{x}=\frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}.\]

Use cumulative frequencies to locate the central observation or observations. An unweighted mean of the listed x-values ignores how often each occurs.

Grouping loses the exact positions

Replace each class by its midpoint m only when estimating moments:

\[\bar{x}\approx\frac{\sum fm}{\sum f},\qquad\sigma^2\approx\frac{\sum fm^2}{\sum f}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\]

The midpoint model has exact calculated moments, but these are estimates of the original raw-data moments. A modal class instead uses frequency density if widths differ.

An unknown frequency belongs in both totals

Keep it in \(\sum f\) and in the weighted sum. Solve the supplied mean condition and reject a negative or non-integer count. Check the denominator is nonzero.

Interpolated grouped medians need an assumption

\[\widehat{Q}_2=L+\frac{N/2-C}{f}\,w.\]

L is the median class lower boundary, C the cumulative count before it, f its frequency and w its width. This assumes uniform within-class spread. Use the stated continuous boundaries and the N/2 cumulative level; the exact median of unknown raw values is not determined.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the observation count, measurement units and requested measure.
  2. Keep exact totals and distinguish raw values from grouped estimates.
  3. Restore every original count, coding or value condition.
  4. State the complete result and justify a contextual choice separately.
mistakes: Use total frequency as the denominator.
Do not treat midpoints as known original observations.
An unknown frequency changes the denominator too.
Separate a median rank, its class and its estimated measurement value.

examples.title: A median is read from cumulative positions
examples.question:
ValueFrequency
12
23
51

Find the mean, median and mode.
examples.solution:
\[n=6,\qquad\bar{x}=\frac{13}{6}.\]

The third and fourth observations are both 2, so the median is 2. The mode is also 2, because its frequency is greatest.

examples.title: Estimate using weighted class midpoints
examples.question:
ClassFrequency
0 ≤ x < 103
10 ≤ x < 205
20 ≤ x < 402

Estimate the mean.
examples.solution:
The midpoints are 5, 15 and 30.

\[\bar{x}\approx\frac{3(5)+5(15)+2(30)}{10}=15.\]

This does not mean every original observation equalled a midpoint.

examples.title: An unknown frequency occurs on both sides
examples.question: Values 1, 3, 5 have frequencies 2, k, 4. Their mean is 3.5. Find k.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{2+3k+20}{6+k}=\frac72\\\Rightarrow\quad44+6k=42+7k.\end{gathered}\]

Thus \(k=2\), giving 8 observations and the required mean. Solving only the numerator would use the wrong count.

examples.title: Read an interpolated median from a grouped model
examples.question: Classes \([0,10),[10,20),[20,40)\) have frequencies 3, 5, 2. Assuming uniform spread in each class, estimate the median.
examples.solution:
The target cumulative level is 5. Before the middle class the count is 3, so

\[\widehat{Q}_2=10+\frac{5-3}{5}(10)=14.\]

The exact raw median cannot be recovered from this table alone.

lessons.title: Weighted means and combined moments
lessons.summary: Combine at most two data sets through compatible totals, keeping within-group and between-group spread distinct.
lessons.objective: Combine at most two data sets through compatible totals, keeping within-group and between-group spread distinct.
lessons.before: Order data, read a frequency table and retain exact fractions. Mixed-topic written tasks also use descriptive variance and SD, introduced in the first lesson.
lessons.ideas:
Weight group means by their counts

\[\bar{x}_{\rm all}=\frac{n_A\bar{x}_A+n_B\bar{x}_B}{n_A+n_B}.\]

The unweighted average works only for equal group sizes or coincident means. For positive group sizes and distinct means, the combined mean lies strictly between them.

Combine square-sums, not SDs

\[S_i=n_i\bar{x}_i,\qquad T_i=n_i(\sigma_i^2+\bar{x}_i^{\,2}).\]\[\sigma_{\rm all}^2=\frac{T_A+T_B}{n_A+n_B}-\bar{x}_{\rm all}^{\,2}.\]

Different group centres add between-group spread. Averaging the SDs misses it. Pooling two observed groups is not the same operation as adding two independent random variables.

A target mean can determine a group size

Keep the unknown size in the total count and the weighted sum. Verify that it is a positive integer and that the target mean is feasible.

Put both groups on a common scale first

Decode different origins or units separately, then combine original totals. Adding two differently coded sums as though they measured the same thing is invalid.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the observation count, measurement units and requested measure.
  2. Keep exact totals and distinguish raw values from grouped estimates.
  3. Restore every original count, coding or value condition.
  4. State the complete result and justify a contextual choice separately.
mistakes: Do not average unequal-size group means without weights.
Never average SDs to obtain a pooled SD.
Between-group differences can increase pooled spread.
Decode both groups to compatible original units before pooling.

examples.title: Unequal groups pull the combined mean unequally
examples.question: Four observations have mean 10 and six have mean 20. Find the combined mean.
examples.solution:
\[\bar{x}=\frac{4(10)+6(20)}{10}=16.\]

The answer is closer to 20 because the second group is larger.

examples.title: Reconstruct both moments before pooling
examples.question: A group of 3 has mean 8 and population SD 2; a group of 2 has mean 13 and population SD 3. Find the combined mean and variance.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}S&=24+26=50,\\T&=3(64+4)+2(169+9)\\&=560.\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=10,\\\sigma^2&=\frac{560}{5}-10^2=12.\end{aligned}\]

Both the within-group spread and the difference of the two centres contribute.

examples.title: Recover an unknown count from a target mean
examples.question: Six values have mean 12. An additional group has mean 18. The combined mean is 16. How many values are in the additional group?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}72+18n=16(6+n)\\\Rightarrow\quad n=12.\end{gathered}\]

The count is a positive integer and the target lies between 12 and 18.

examples.title: Different coding origins need separate decoding
examples.question: Group A has 4 values with \(\sum(x-10)=8\); B has 6 values with \(\sum(y-20)=-12\). Both measure the same quantity. Find the combined mean.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}S_A&=48,\\S_B&=108,\\\bar{x}_{\rm all}&=\frac{156}{10}=15.6.\end{aligned}\]

The sum of the two coded totals, −4, would not be an original measurement total.

lessons.title: Corrected records, missing observations and reverse problems
lessons.summary: Update counts and both moments together, then use independent conditions to recover unknown records or constraints.
lessons.objective: Update counts and both moments together, then use independent conditions to recover unknown records or constraints.
lessons.before: Order data, read a frequency table and retain exact fractions. Mixed-topic written tasks also use descriptive variance and SD, introduced in the first lesson.
lessons.ideas:
Correcting a value changes two totals

If a was entered but should have been b,

\[\begin{aligned}S_{\rm new}&=S-a+b,\\T_{\rm new}&=T-a^2+b^2.\end{aligned}\]

The count stays the same. Remove the erroneous square; do not add the square of the correction.

Adding or removing a record also changes n

Adjust n, S and T together before recalculating mean and variance. An unchanged mean does not imply an unchanged SD. If one value was counted twice, remove precisely one duplicate.

Two unknown records need two moment conditions

Use the new mean to find their sum and the new variance to reconstruct their square-sum. Solve both conditions, give the requested ordered pair and restore the original equations.

A variance constraint can become a quadratic

Adding one unknown real observation makes the new mean and variance depend on that observation. Complete the square to find a minimum or solve an exact interval condition. This is a mixed application of 9709 P1 Quadratics; no differentiation is needed.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the observation count, measurement units and requested measure.
  2. Keep exact totals and distinguish raw values from grouped estimates.
  3. Restore every original count, coding or value condition.
  4. State the complete result and justify a contextual choice separately.
mistakes: For a correction use b²−a², not (b−a)².
Removal changes the count as well as the totals.
An unchanged mean does not establish unchanged variance.
Keep both roots or the complete allowed interval, subject to the original restrictions.

examples.title: A correction need not change the SD
examples.question: Five records have mean 12 and square-sum 800. One recorded 8 should be 18. Find the corrected mean and SD.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}S_{\rm new}&=60-8+18=70,\\T_{\rm new}&=800-64+324\\&=1060.\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}\bar{x}_{\rm new}&=14,\\\sigma_{\rm new}&=\sqrt{212-196}=4.\end{aligned}\]

The old SD was also 4. This is a property of these data, not a general rule for corrections.

examples.title: Remove the observation and its place in the count
examples.question: Six observations have sum 48 and square-sum 430. Remove one observation of 8. Find the remaining mean and variance.
examples.solution:
\[n=5,\quad S=40,\quad T=366.\]\[\bar{x}=8,\qquad\sigma^2=\frac{366}{5}-64=\frac{46}{5}.\]

The mean remains 8, but the variance has changed.

examples.title: Two added values are linked, not separate guesses
examples.question: Add a and b to 3, 4, 6, 7. The six values then have mean 6 and variance 5. Find \(a
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}a+b&=36-20=16,\\a^2+b^2&=6(5+36)-110\\&=136.\end{aligned}\]

Substituting \(b=16-a\) gives roots 6 and 10. The ordered answer is \((a,b)=(6,10)\).

examples.title: Complete the variance square
examples.question: Add a real value t to 2, 4, 6. Find the smallest possible population variance and all t for which it is at most 5.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{aligned}V(t)&=\frac{56+t^2}{4}-\left(\frac{12+t}{4}\right)^2\\&=2+\frac3{16}(t-4)^2.\end{aligned}\]

The minimum is 2 at \(t=4\). The inequality reduces to \((t-4)^2\le16\), giving \(0\le t\le8\). The existing unequal observations prevent a zero minimum variance.

questions.title: Calibration measurements
questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Measures of variation: descriptive variance and standard deviation.

The following 10 measurements are recorded in millimetres.

Observations
30, 28, 23, 30, 29, 27, 23, 24
34, 33

  1. Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the data.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The number of observations is \(10\).

\[\sum x=281,\qquad\sum x^2=8033.\]\[\bar x=\frac{281}{10}=28.1,\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{8033}{10}-(28.1)^2=13.69.\]

Taking the positive square root gives \(3.7\).
questions.hint_html: Keep exact totals until the final calculation.

questions.title: Consistency of output
questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Measures of variation: descriptive variance and standard deviation.

The numbers of items completed in each of eight equal-length sessions by machine A are shown below.

Observations
9, 15, 20, 24, 28, 32, 35, 37

For machine B, the mean is \(28\) and the standard deviation is \(\frac{\sqrt{42}}{2}\).

  1. Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the output of machine A.

    [3]

  2. State which machine has more consistent output. Give a reason.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The number of observations is \(8\).

\[\sum x=200,\qquad\sum x^2=5684.\]\[\bar x=\frac{200}{8}=25,\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{5684}{8}-(25)^2=85.5.\]

Taking the positive square root gives \(\frac{3 \sqrt{38}}{2}\approx 9.25\).

(b)

Machine B has standard deviation \(\frac{\sqrt{42}}{2}\approx 3.24\), smaller than \(\frac{3 \sqrt{38}}{2}\approx 9.25\) for A. Smaller spread in the same units means more consistent output; a higher mean alone would not show greater consistency.
questions.hint_html: Consistency concerns variation, not the size of the mean.

(a)

For a small numerical data set, a stem-and-leaf diagram retains the individual values and makes their order and overall shape visible.

(c)

A few very long delays affect the magnitudes used in the mean. The median depends on ordered position and is less affected by those extremes.

questions.title: One observation withdrawn
questions.prompt_html:
All stated summary values are exact unless described as estimates. Keep unrounded intermediate totals. Descriptive variance and SD use divisor n, not n−1. Non-exact numerical answers: 3 significant figures; exact equivalent forms are accepted.

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Measures of variation: descriptive variance and standard deviation.

A sample of 17 lengths \(x\) centimetres has

\[\sum x=559,\qquad\sum x^2=18849.\]

  1. Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the data.

    [3]

  2. One observation is withdrawn. The mean of the remaining 16 lengths is \(32\) cm. Find the withdrawn length and the new standard deviation.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Mean \(\frac{559}{17}\approx 32.9\); standard deviation \(\frac{4 \sqrt{497}}{17}\approx 5.25\).

(b)

Withdrawn length \(47\text{ cm}\); new standard deviation \(4\text{ cm}\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The number of observations is \(17\).

\[\sum x=559,\qquad\sum x^2=18849.\]\[\bar x=\frac{559}{17}=\frac{559}{17},\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{18849}{17}-(\frac{559}{17})^2=\frac{7952}{289}.\]

Taking the positive square root gives \(\frac{4 \sqrt{497}}{17}\approx 5.25\).

(b)

\[r=559-16(32)=47.\]\[\sigma_{\rm new}^2=\frac{18849-47^2}{16}-32^2=16.\]

Thus the standard deviation is \(4\) cm. Remove the square of the withdrawn value, not the value itself, from the square total.

A sample of 19 lengths \(x\) centimetres has

    [3]

Mean \(\frac{682}{19}\approx 35.9\); standard deviation \(\frac{6 \sqrt{382}}{19}\approx 6.17\).

Withdrawn length \(52\text{ cm}\); new standard deviation \(5\text{ cm}\).

(a)

The number of observations is \(19\).

Taking the positive square root gives \(\frac{6 \sqrt{382}}{19}\approx 6.17\).

(b)

\[r=682-18(35)=52.\]\[\sigma_{\rm new}^2=\frac{25204-52^2}{18}-35^2=25.\]

Thus the standard deviation is \(5\) cm. Remove the square of the withdrawn value, not the value itself, from the square total.

The coefficient of the square is positive. The square vanishes exactly when \(y=25\), giving minimum variance \(8\).

(c)

\[\frac{8}{81}(y-25)^2\leq \frac{32}{9}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(y-25)^2\leq 36.\]

Taking both bounds and including equality gives \(19\leq y\leq 31\).

  3. Find all values of \(y\) for which \(V\leq \frac{1860}{49}\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The original sum and square total are \(740\) and \(28100\). The new mean is \(\frac{740+y}{21}\). Hence

\[V=\frac{28100+y^2}{21}-\left(\frac{740+y}{21}\right)^2.\]

Expanding and completing the square gives

\[V=\frac{240}{7}+\frac{20}{441}(y-37)^2.\]

(b)

The coefficient of the square is positive. The square vanishes exactly when \(y=37\), giving minimum variance \(\frac{240}{7}\).

(c)

\[\frac{20}{441}(y-37)^2\leq \frac{180}{49}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(y-37)^2\leq 81.\]

Taking both bounds and including equality gives \(28\leq y\leq 46\).
questions.hint_html: Use the new totals to write the variance as a quadratic in y, then complete the square; differentiation is not needed.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses the new count in both terms of the variance formula.
Expands and completes the square in y.
Substitutes the upper bound and isolates the square.

conventions.variance: Descriptive variance uses divisor n, not n−1.
conventions.rounding: Give non-exact numerical answers to 3 significant figures; keep unrounded intermediate totals. Exact equivalent answers are accepted.
conventions.quartiles: For ungrouped data: medians of the lower and upper halves, excluding the overall middle observation when n is odd. This is stated as a bank convention, not an assertion that all published papers use one convention.
conventions.grouped_data: Use class midpoints for mean and standard-deviation estimates. Median interpolation assumes uniform within-class spread, stated when required.
conventions.summaries: All stated summary values are exact unless explicitly described as estimates.

Use population descriptive variance with divisor n. M marks reward a relevant method even when later arithmetic is wrong; A marks follow a relevant method.
